transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

Since I stopped working full-time, I keep starting projects for the museum and then just never finishing them, even when I really want to. I've always had a tendency to "zone out," but lately it's gotten so disruptive that I worried it might be early cognitive decline, so my doctor referred me here to get it checked out.
Can you describe how your difficulty with focus or 'zoning out' affects your daily tasks? Have these problems been present since childhood or did they start more recently?

Honestly, this goes all the way back to elementary school, where my teachers always said I was bright but constantly daydreaming and forgetting my homework. It has become much more disruptive since I retired from my handyman job; now I drift off during museum planning meetings, get sidetracked mid-task, and have even double-booked rooms. It really makes me feel unreliable because I just can't seem to keep track of the details without my old routine.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or lost interest in activities you used to enjoy, especially during periods when your focus problems got worse?

No, I wouldn't say I feel down or hopeless, and I definitely haven't lost interest in my hobbies—I still really want to do them and enjoy them. It's more that I get incredibly frustrated with myself because I want to do these projects so badly, but I just can't seem to stay focused enough to finish them.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F90", "F32", "F33"], but based on this conversation, F32 (episode of mild or moderate depressive disorder) and F33 (recurrent depressive disorder) seem unlikely because the patient explicitly denies feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in activities. The lifelong pattern of attentional difficulties starting in childhood, significant inattention and distractibility without mood disturbance, and functional impairment in multiple settings—especially now post-retirement—strongly support a neurodevelopmental origin. The persistent 'zoning out,' history of daydreaming, and executive dysfunction despite preserved motivation align best with F90 (hyperkinetic disorder), which includes presentations of predominantly inattentive ADHD. No new symptoms suggest other conditions, so F90 remains the most plausible candidate.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a lifelong pattern of inattention and distractibility, with onset in childhood and persistent functional impairment in adulthood, particularly evident in task completion and organization, meeting criteria for ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation. Mood symptoms are absent, ruling out depressive disorder as a primary cause.
